power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A power analysis carried out in G*power (Faul et al., 2007) suggested that for an interaction between trial type and memory-load group, a total sample size of 56 subjects would be needed based on effect size of f=0.16, an alpha level of .05, power of 0.8 (with G*power defaults of 0.5 for correlation between repeated measures and 1 for non-sphericity correction). Based on previous studies, we assumed that we would need to exclude around 15% of participants and thus aimed to test at least 32 in each group.
table.statistical_test_other: interaction between trial type and memory-load group

table.text: We aimed to test until we had 33 participants in each group. In Experiment 1, we found the expected two-way interaction-effect between memory-load group and value-congruence in the test-phase with effect size ηp² = 0.07. Based on this, we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size using G*Power (v3.1) with the following parameters: effect size ηp² = 0.07 (f = 0.39), alpha level = .01, power = .90, number of groups = 2, measurements = 4, correlation among repeated measures = 0 (to be conservative, actual r = .14 -.74) and nonsphericity correction of 1. table.title: Does working memory load shift the balance from goal-directed to habitual behaviour?
table.authors: Tim van Timmeren, sanne de wit, Sharene Klein
table.description:
Goal-directed behavior is mediated by the anticipation of a desirable outcome. According to certain two-process theories, extensive behavioral repetition leads to a shift from flexible, goal-directed control over instrumental actions to inflexible, outcome-insensitive habits (de Wit & Dickinson, 2009; Dickinson & Balleine, 1994; Heyes & Dickinson, 1990). Outcome-devaluation procedures assess the ability to adjust one’s behavior to a sudden decrease in outcome desirability (Adams & Dickinson, 1981; Balleine & O’Doherty, 2010; Dickinson, 1985). 
Previous research indicates that cognitive working memory (WM) resources contribute to the extent to which individuals are capable of flexibly controlling their behavior: taxing the WM system during decision making impairs goal-directed control (Otto et al, 2013), and high baseline WM-capacity has been shown to protect against the effects of stress on habitual responding (Otto et al, 2013, PNAS; Quaedflieg et al, 2019). However, the effect of WM-load on goal-directed control has never been tested using an outcome devaluation paradigm. Using a novel a new computerized instrumental learning task, we will investigate whether performing a secondary WM-task affects the balance between goal-directed and habitual responding.
table.research_questions:
In the current study, we aim to investigate whether WM load affects the ability to flexibly adjust responding to discriminative stimuli depending on the current outcome value. 

Hypotheses
1.	If training results in increased habitual responding during test, then participants will make more responses towards devalued outcomes (commission errors) than towards still not valuable outcomes; and they will make less responses to upvalued outcomes (omission errors) than towards still valuable outcomes after outcome revaluation.
2.	Importantly, if WM-load affects habitual responding, the number of commission errors (after devaluation) and
3.	The number of omission errors (after upvaluation) will be larger for in the WM load group, than in the no WM load group.
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.q7: Participants are not aware that the study involves a WM-load manipulation
table.study_design_overview: This is a two-group, repeated measures mixed design, with the within-subject factors value and congruency and the between-subject factor WM-load
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will be mostly students, aged between 18-35 years old and recruited through the online system of the university. They will be paid €15 or 1.5 points for their participation.
table.sample_size: We continue testing until 64 participants (32/group) have been tested (independent of exclusions)
table.sample_size_rationale: A total sample size of 56 subjects would be needed based on an effect size of f=0.16, an alpha level of .05 and power of 0.8 (computed using G*Power). Based on our previous experience, we expect to exclude 10% of the participants on the basis of performance following our exclusion criteria. To be on the safe side, we will continue data collecting until 32 participants for each group have participated. The effect size was obtained from a similar previous study (Otto et al, 2013, Psychological Science; experiment 2) that used a between-subject WM-load manipulation (Table 2, Load x Reward x Transition Type interaction).
table.manipulated_variables: WM-load will be manipulated during the test phase of the Sneaky Skate Game using the numerical Stroop task; participants in the no WM-load condition will simpy be asked to make a left or right press. Durations of the various stages of the trial will be kept the same between conditions.
table.measured_variables:
The main outcome variable will be percentage response rates, measured during the training phase (to ensure that participants learn the associations) and during the test phase to measure habitual responding (reflected by the value X congruency interaction). 

General working memory capacity will be measured using the Digit Span as measured by Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale IV.
table.indices: Response rates will be calculated by the number of responses divided by the total number of trials in that condition
table.statistical_tests:
We will use a 2x2x2 mixed ANOVA to analyze our results, with response rates being our dependent variable. The mixed ANOVA includes the within-subject factors value (valuable, non-valuable) and congruency (value during test congruent/incongruent with value during training) and the between-subject factor WM-load. Habitual responding will be reflected by the interaction between value and congruency, where:  
1.	The number of responses is higher for nonvaluable-incongruent (i.e. devalued) outcomes than nonvaluable-congruent (i.e. still not valuable) outcomes.
2.	The number of responses is higher for valuable-congruent (i.e. still not valuable) outcomes than valuable-incongruent (i.e. upvalued) outcomes.
The effect of WM-load on habitual responding will be reflected by a 3-way interaction between test outcome value, congruence, and WM-load, driven by:
4.	A higher number of responses for the nonvaluable-incongruent (i.e. devalued) outcomes for the WMload group than the no WMload group
5.	A lower number of responses for the valuable-incongruent (i.e. upvalued) outcomes for the WMload group than the no WMload group

Additionally, we expect a negative correlation between baseline WM-capacity (measured using the WAIS Digit Span) and habitual responding on the SSG (reflected by the 2 habit indexes), which will be moderated by WM-load such that this effect is more pronounced under WM-load than no WM-load.
table.transformations:
For the training phase, average response-counts per 2 blocks will be entered into a repeated-measures ANOVA with factors Block (18) and Outcome value (valuable, not valuable). Average reaction times per 2 blocks (one odd and one even) for the trials on which a correct response is made will be entered into a repeated measures ANOVA with factor Block (18).
For the test phase, scores will be collapsed across blocks. 
For the regression analysis with SSG performance, we will compute two difference scores: [still valuable - upvalued] (=habit index of valuable stimuli) and [devalued - still not valuable] (=habit index of non-valuable stimuli).
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<.05 criteria for determining if the the ANOVA and the post hoc test suggest that the results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. The post-hoc Tukey-Kramer test adjusts for multiple comparisons.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
•	To assure that participants have learned the correct associations between vans, responses, and ice creams before the test starts, data of participants that do not reach an average accuracy of 80% in the last four blocks of training will be excluded.
•	To assure that participants have noticed and understood the changes in value of the ice creams during the test phase, data of participants that do not respond at least 25% to stimuli that were not associated with a response during training but are associated with a response during the test (upvalued) will be excluded.
table.missing_data_handling: If data from a subject on the SSG is not complete, that subject will not be included in the analysis.
table.exploratory_analyses: We will explore the relationship between automaticity (measured using the SRBAI) and performance on the SSG and WM-capacity (digit span).

live_data_statements: Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulusresponse association learned during training was no longer appropriate.

In fact, two recent studies have concluded that when participants are instructed to withhold responses for some stimuli, interference from S-R associations can only be observed for highly consolidated mappings shaped by lifelong real-world reinforcement such as green-go and red-stop (Ceceli et al., 2020; Du & Haith, 2023).
Participants are required to learn the specific outcome associated with each stimulus during training because only some outcomes are valuable during each block.
During the test phase, the value of associated outcomes could change and participants had to choose whether to respond to stimuli on the basis of the associated outcome value.
After half of the trials, the participants were then asked to recall and respond to one of the digits.
In total, 63 participants were recruited from the University of Amsterdam participant website.
At the start of every block, during both training and test phases, participants were instructed on which ice creams they should be collecting in that block using an outcome value instruction screen.

Participants had to select the two ice creams that were valuable in the upcoming block and if they got it incorrect then the outcome value instruction screen and test were repeated until they were correct.
Once the vehicle started moving, the participant had 600ms to push the spacebar if they wished to collect the ice cream outcome that was associated with that stimulus.

If the participant had pushed the space bar to collect the ice cream within the allotted 600ms, the skateboarder moved down to intercept the vehicle as it approached the right-hand side of the screen.
If the participant had not responded within the initial 600ms (before the ice cream appeared) then the vehicle and ice cream continued off screen and the skateboarder missed the intercept point.
Participants were given 300ms to remember the numbers as well as their relative physical size and their relative location.

After completion of the SORT trial, participants were prompted on 50% of trials to report either the number larger in size or value, by pressing a left or right key that corresponded to the location of the digit in question (see Figure 2C).
Participants had 1000ms to make their response and were told 'too late' if they did not respond in time, but no feedback was given about the accuracy of their response.
In both conditions, participants were told they would earn an additional point when making the correct response and lose a point for the incorrect response.

In the forward digit-span test the participant was required to repeat each sequence back exactly as it had been read, in the backwards test the participants had to repeat the sequence in reverse order.
In the sequencing task the participant had to repeat the sequence in order of size.

This answer was highlighted and then participants were required to answer one question on how difficult it would be to change that response ("This response is something … that would be difficult to change"), followed by the four questions from the SRBAI e.g.
Participants were told that they were going to play the "Sneaky Skateboard Game" where they were playing as a skateboarder and had to collect as many ice creams (and points) as possible.
Prior to the instrumental training phase participants completed a short demo with discriminative stimuli (vehicles) that did not appear in the real task.

Participants were told that the outcomes would no longer be visible because the drivers put an advertisement on top, and that the pizza's they had to collect differed from the first part of practice (i.e. some were devalued and some upvalued).
In total, participants completed 36 training blocks, resulting in a total of 576 training trials and 72 stimulus-response repetitions per stimulus.
Every 6 blocks, participants were allowed to take a break of 30 seconds and could resume the task at any time during that period by pressing the space bar.
Next, participants were instructed that, just like before, they would be informed at the beginning of each block as to which ice creams they needed to collect.
Participants were also told that they were still earning points for collecting valuable ice creams (and losing points for collecting not-valuable ice creams).
When participants had completed the four test blocks, they were informed as to the total points they had won.

As expected, participants were better on Stroopcongruent trials (25% of memory trials where the numerical value and physical size of the digit-to-be-reported were compatible; accuracy of 76%, SEM: 5%) relative to the Stroopincongruent trials (75% of memory-trials, mean accuracy 64%, SEM: 4%).

Participants were less accurate on both devalued trials (where they had to now inhibit the Go response) and upvalued trials (where a Go response was now required), relative to trials where the value of the outcome signalled by the cue was congruent with that during training.

Participants were more accurate on Stroopcongruent trials (25% of all memory trials; mean accuracy of 83%, SEM: 3%) relative to the Stroop-incongruent trials (75% of all memory trials; mean accuracy of 75%, SEM: 4%).
Participants were less accurate on both devalued and upvalued trials relative to still-not-valuable and still-valuable trials respectively.

In the slips-of-action task, a variant of the outcome devaluation paradigm, all outcomes are valuable during the instrumental learning phase, meaning that participants are not required to learn the S-O associations to perform well (Buabang et al., 2021; De Houwer et al., 2018).

We did not observe any effects of working memory load on the valuable Go trials at testspecifically, there was no indication that load impaired performance on upvalued trials (where participants had to carry out a response in the presence of a stimulus that had been trained as NoGo).

Specifically, following instrumental training, Wood et al. (2023) presented participants with an outcome (labelled 'goal-directed cue' that participants were instructed to respond to; O-R) and following a delay, an irrelevant 'stimulus cue' (which could trigger either a congruent or incongruent response; S-R).

Increased slips of action for overtrained stimuli may be observed when participants are under working memory load, thus providing direct evidence for stronger habits, as predicted by the associative dual-process model.
In total, 69 participants were recruited from the University of Amsterdam participant website, following the recruitment protocol of Experiment 1.
Six participants were excluded from all analyses (see results) leaving 63 participants in the analysis.

Including all six possible block combinations of stimuli signalling two valuable and two not-valuable outcomes is different to our previous study where participants had blocks in which the same four stimuli were repeated in alternating fashion(Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: Despite our familiarity with the concept of habits, eliciting and measuring habitual "slips of action" experimentally in humans has proven to be difficult.

A possible explanation is that participants in psychological experiments actively recruit goal-directed control and therefore make few habitual slips-of-action in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes.
In the current experiment we used the Symmetrical Outcome Revaluation Task in combination with a working memory load in an attempt to tip the balance from goal-directed control to habitual control.

During the instrumental learning phase, participants learned to make a Go response to stimuli signalling valuable outcomes (and points) while not responding (NoGo) to stimuli signalling not-valuable outcomes.
During the subsequent test phase, the outcomes signalled by the stimuli were either value-congruent with training (stillvaluable and still-not-valuable), or value-incongruent (devalued and upvalued).
Participants had to flexibly adjust their behaviour on value-incongruent trials where the stimulusresponse association learned during training was no longer appropriate.
For half the participants, a concurrent working memory load was imposed during the test phase.

In line with our preregistered hypotheses, participants showed evidence for habitual slips of action across two experiments, but those under working memory load showed increased habitual responding (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses in the presence of stimuli signalling devalued outcomes).
This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans.
The term 'habit' is used frequently in everyday language to refer to behaviours that are learnt via behavioural repetition and carried out relatively automatically.

Influential accounts of habit in human behaviour consistently emphasise the role of stable cue-response associations, automaticity, and reduced reliance on deliberative goal evaluation (de Wit & Dickinson, 2009; Gardner et al., 2024; Mazar & W. Wood, 2018; Verplanken & Orbell, 2003; W. Wood & Rünger, 2016).

text.text: Sometimes these habits are adaptive (e.g., regularly going to the gym at the same time each day) but at other times they can be maladaptive (e.g., regularly eating chocolate on the couch at the same time each day).

The associative dual-process model of behaviour defines habits as responses (R) that are elicited by contexts and stimuli (S), regardless of the current desirability of the outcome (de Wit & Dickinson, 2009; Dickinson, 1994 Dickinson, , 2016)).

text.text: These can be contrasted with goal-directed actions, driven by anticipation of and current desire for the outcome (O).

Goal-directed behaviour allows for flexible behavioural adjustments when goals change, but at the same time may be relatively cognitively demanding because the expected outcome requires evaluation before the corresponding action is carried out (O-R) 1 .
text.formatted: Goal-directed behaviour allows for flexible behavioural adjustments when goals change, but at the same time may be relatively cognitively demanding because the expected outcome requires evaluation before the corresponding action is carried out (O-R) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">1</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, habits are mediated by S-R associations, such that these responses are triggered by contexts or stimuli without evaluation of the current desirability of the consequences and can be carried out quickly with relatively little cognitive effort.

Importantly, the dual-process account does not require either form of control to be regarded as the default; rather, behaviour may reflect the relative contribution of S-R and outcome-mediated processes, with the balance between them influenced by the conditions under which behaviour is generated.
In the lab, S-R habits have been extensively studied in both rodents and humans using the outcome-devaluation paradigm (Adams, 1982; Balleine & O'Doherty, 2010; Dickinson, 1985).
text.formatted: In the lab, S-R habits have been extensively studied in both rodents and humans using the outcome-devaluation paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Adams, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Balleine & O'Doherty, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Dickinson, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: In the human version, subjects learn that different responses earn different outcomes during the initial instrumental training phase (e.g., a left key press leads to chocolate, a right key press to popcorn).
One of these outcomes is then devalued,commonly through instructed devaluation, satiation, or by adding bitter solutions to food.
Sensitivity to outcome devaluation is then assessed in an extinction test.
If the participant flexibly reduces responding on the key that leads to the devalued (relative to the valuable) outcome, then behaviour is under goal-directed control (O-R).
By contrast, a failure to reduce responding on the key associated with the devalued outcome is interpreted as an S-R habit.
However, revealing human habits in the lab using the outcome devaluation paradigm has proven to be challenging.

Healthy participants perform exceptionally well in the outcome devaluation test (de Wit et al., 2018; Morris et al., 2015; van Timmeren et al., 2020; Watson, van Wingen, et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: Although they do make some erroneous stimulus-elicited "slips of action" towards devalued outcomes (relative to valuable outcomes), in general they are quite capable of flexibly adjusting their behaviour after changes in outcome value (Watson, van Wingen, et al., 2018).

text.text: There are several factors that could tip the balance towards goal-directed control rather than habits in human outcome devaluation tasks.
One obvious possibility is that the amount of training offered to participants is typically brief; less than one hour in a single session.
This single-session training may result in relatively weak S-R associations that are easier to overcome when the outcome is no longer desirable.

However, recent studies that have used extensive training protocols (across days or weeks) with humans and examined short-versus long-trained stimuli have not found evidence that longer relative to shorter training leads to increased 'slips of action' at test following devaluation (de Wit et al., 2018; Du & Haith, 2023; Luque et al., 2020; Pool et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: Another potential reason that participants make few overt slips of action for devalued outcomes is that goal-directed control may re-emerge during the test phase, obscuring the measurement of S-R habits.

It has been proposed that the context switch between training and test phases in human outcome-devaluation tasks may cause goal-directed processes to re-emerge to control responding during the test phase, thus reducing the likelihood of erroneous slips of action (de Wit et al., 2018; Watson & de Wit, 2018; W. text.text: Another reason that laboratory studies with outcome devaluation tasks likely underestimate the expression of habitual control, is that they are usually performed in the absence of distraction and competing cognitive demands.
Under those conditions, participants may be perfectly capable of keeping current goals and action-outcome contingencies active in working memory.
Indeed, some of the conditions under which habits typically emerge in everyday life involve some form of depletion of cognitive resources.
To illustrate, a previous study examined whether depletion of cognitive resources would lead to an increase in reallife habitual behaviours (Neal et al., 2013).
text.formatted: To illustrate, a previous study examined whether depletion of cognitive resources would lead to an increase in reallife habitual behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Neal et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Across a series of experiments, participants first reported on their baseline habitual behaviours and were then surveyed again on days where cognitive resources were assumed to be depleted (e.g., during exam weeks or when asked to repeatedly use their non-dominant hand throughout the day).
Participants reported engaging more frequently in habitual behaviours (e.g., eating certain types of food) on 'depletion' days compared to 'ordinary' (non-depletion) days.
These findings provide important ecological evidence that limitations on cognitive resources are linked to greater reliance on habitual action selection.
However, self-report measures of habit frequency cannot directly dissociate habitual control from changes in goals, motivation, or opportunity.

Outcome devaluation paradigms therefore complement this approach by offering a rigorous test of habitual control, allowing behaviour to be assessed when outcome values are experimentally manipulated, and other factors held constant.

While the effect of a working memory load on test performance in the outcome devaluation paradigm has not been investigated yet, several strands of indirect evidence suggest that this is a promising approach to revealing habits in an experimental setting.

Firstly, disruption to working memory has been seen to reduce the ability to exhibit flexible declarative knowledge in an associative learning task (Foerde et al., 2006) and bias behaviour toward repeating prior responses in a voluntary task switching paradigm (Demanet et al., 2010).

Finally, individual differences in baseline working memory capacity have been related to the ability of participants to exert goal-directed control and flexibly adjust behaviour following changes in outcome value in this task (Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: In the present study, we therefore investigated directly whether introducing a concurrent working memory load during the test phase shifts the relative expression of goal-directed control and habits in the outcome devaluation task.

To this end, we used the Symmetrical Outcome Revaluation Task (SORT: Watson et al., 2023), which incorporates both outcome devaluation and outcome appreciation (i.e., upvaluation), to study the balance between goaldirected and habitual control.
text.formatted: To this end, we used the Symmetrical Outcome Revaluation Task (SORT: <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Watson et al., 2023)</ref>, which incorporates both outcome devaluation and outcome appreciation (i.e., upvaluation), to study the balance between goaldirected and habitual control.

text.text: Participants learn during the instrumental training phase the correct responses that should be made in the presence of discriminative stimuli in order to earn specific outcomes (and points).
Half of the outcomes are valuable, requiring that they be collected (a "Go" response), and the other half are not valuable, meaning that the participant should withhold responding ("NoGo").
Participants are required to learn the specific outcome associated with each stimulus during training because only some outcomes are valuable during each block.

As a result, participants cannot maximise their earnings in the first few blocks through simple S-R associations ("to this stimulus I respond") -instead they need to monitor the values of the outcomes they are earning and are initially forced to learn the S-O-R associations ("this stimulus signals outcome Y, which is currently worth points so I should respond").
However, the extensive repetition of consistent S-R associations across training blocks ensures that S-R associations are concurrently learned.

During the test phase (conducted in extinction in which no feedback is given), discriminative stimuli are presented, and participants must quickly decide whether to respond (for valuable outcomes) or to inhibit responding (for not-valuable outcomes).
They are instructed that some outcome values change compared to the training phase.
The symmetrical design of the task means that the value of outcomes associated with half of the stimuli changes relative to training (see Figure 1A).
text.formatted: The symmetrical design of the task means that the value of outcomes associated with half of the stimuli changes relative to training (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: For these stimuli, the associated outcome is now either devalued (in contrast to training when they were always valuable) or upvalued (now valuable when they were never valuable during training), and previously learned S-R associations can compete for behavioural control.
As a baseline control condition, the other half of stimuli have outcomes that do not change value between training and test.
As such, the S-R mappings can be relied upon during the test phase.

Importantly, performance on still-not-valuable trials, where participants can rely on learnt S-R "NoGo" associations, is contrasted with performance on devalued trials -which also require response inhibition but lack this benefit of consistent S-R mappings.

This therefore controls for an individual's propensity to withhold responding during the test phase, ensuring that poorer performance on devalued trials is not simply due to a greater propensity to (not) respond.
Instead, a selective impairment on devalued trials reflects greater difficulty using updated outcome information to flexibly adjust behaviour.

Likewise, performance on still-valuable trials can be compared to upvalued trials -both require a Go response, but that was only the learned response for the stimuli signalling still-valuable outcomes.

Furthermore, although habit is often conceptualised in terms of errors of commission, it is also theoretically possible that learned S-R associations contribute to errors of omission when particular stimuli were consistently associated with withholding a response (i.e. a NoGo response; Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Kühn & Brass, 2010).

text.text: Thus, when a stimulus previously associated with a non-valuable outcome now signals a valuable outcome, responding may require greater reliance on goal-directed control to overcome the previously learned NoGo response.

With the SORT, it has been shown that learnt S-R associations induce errors during incongruent trials of the test phase, despite participants having intact explicit knowledge of the appropriate S-O relations (Hennessy et al., 2025; van de Vijver et al., 2023; van Timmeren et al., 2023; Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: We used a between-groups design to examine whether working memory load during the test phase would impact goal-directed control and allow S-R associations to be more prominent.

Participants first underwent instrumental training to learn the outcomes associated with discriminative stimuli and to acquire consistent responding towards the 50% of stimuli associated with valuable outcomes.
During the test phase, the value of associated outcomes could change and participants had to choose whether to respond to stimuli on the basis of the associated outcome value.
For participants in the memory-load group, each test trial began with two numbers with varying features that needed to be remembered.
The test trial of the SORT was then completed.
After half of the trials, the participants were then asked to recall and respond to one of the digits.

Requiring responses on only half of the memory trials ensured that the proportion of responses in the memory test was consistent with the overall proportion of Go responses (i.e. 50%) across the SORT.
For participants in the no-memoryload group, no numbers were displayed before each trial.
However, on half of the SORT trials they were prompted to press a left or right key after they had completed the trial.

We assessed explicit knowledge of all task contingencies at the end of the experiment and also measured working memory capacity, to examine whether individual differences in working memory capacity would affect performance in the task (particularly under working memory load).

Our preregistered hypotheses were that increased reliance on habit responding would be reflected as reduced accuracy on value-incongruent test trials (devalued and upvalued) relative to value-congruent trials (still-not-valuable and still-valuable, respectively).
We also expected that these effects would be exaggerated for those under memory load with poorer performance on the devalued (and upvalued) trials relative to participants in the no-memoryload group.
Finally, we expected a negative correlation between baseline working memory capacity and our indices of habit, and expected this effect to be more pronounced under memory load.
All measures and manipulations are disclosed in the present manuscript.
The aims, hypotheses, methods and analyses were preregistered prior to data collection (osf.io/yrh5p).
We aimed to test until we had 32 participants in each group.

A pre-registered sample size of 64 was arrived at based on the effect size (f = 0.16) found in a previous study using a between-groups working memory load manipulation and a reinforcement learning task used to index goal-directed (model-based) control (Otto, Gershman, et al., 2013, Experiment 2).

text.text: At the beginning of the trial a cartoon skateboarder was also presented at the top of the screen.
Once the vehicle started moving, the participant had 600ms to push the spacebar if they wished to collect the ice cream outcome that was associated with that stimulus.
At 600ms (when the vehicle was halfway across the screen) the associated ice cream appeared on top of the vehicle.

If the participant had pushed the space bar to collect the ice cream within the allotted 600ms, the skateboarder moved down to intercept the vehicle as it approached the right-hand side of the screen.
The ice cream was then left behind with the skate boarder as the vehicle continued, passing off screen at 1200ms.
If the participant had not responded within the initial 600ms (before the ice cream appeared) then the vehicle and ice cream continued off screen and the skateboarder missed the intercept point.

Each block of instrumental training consisted of 16 trials in which two stimuli associated with valuable ice creams and two stimuli associated with not-valuable ice creams were each presented four times in total.

text.text: Across training blocks therefore, each ice cream was equally often valuable as not valuable.

Crucially, however, the value assigned to each van stimulus (and accordingly, the associated 'Go' or 'NoGo' response) was consistent throughout the entire training phase allowing for the development of S-R associative links.
The test phase trials were very similar, with each block beginning with instructions as to which ice creams should be collected.

The critical test phase manipulation was that all stimuli now appeared in the same block (i.e. both stimuli associated with an ice cream appeared whereas during training they had never appeared in the same block).

Because all the vans appeared intermixed during the test phase, it meant that the value of the signalled outcome was congruent with the training value for half of the stimuli but incongruent for the other half.
This resulted in four different trial types per block of the test phase (as depicted in Figure 1A).

text.text: Congruent trials were either 'still-valuable' (the stimulus consistently signalled a valuable outcome across both training and test) or 'still-not-valuable' (stimuli that were consistently signalling a not-valuable outcome across training and test).

By contrast, incongruent trials could be either 'upvalued' (stimuli that had consistently signalled a notvaluable ice cream during training, but now signalled a valuable ice cream during test) or 'devalued' (stimuli that had always signalled a valuable ice cream during training, but now signalled a not-valuable ice cream).
Within each test block, each of the eight stimuli were presented four times, with trial order randomized per 16 trials (32 trials total per block).
During the test phase the associated ice cream was never shown to the participant (to prevent further learning during the test phase).

text.text: The experimenter read out a series of digits of increasing length at the rate of one digit per second.

In the forward digit-span test the participant was required to repeat each sequence back exactly as it had been read, in the backwards test the participants had to repeat the sequence in reverse order.
In the sequencing task the participant had to repeat the sequence in order of size.
Sequences started from three digits to a maximum of eight digits (two sequences of each length were included, 12 in total).
Each test was stopped if participants made two consecutive errors.
Participants received one point for each correct answer with a higher score indicating higher working memory capacity.
We used the backwards span task as the measure of working memory capacity.
The backwards span has good reliability and consistency and is closely related to performance on other working memory tasks (Waters & Caplan, 2003).

text.text: The items correspond to the degree to which a behaviour begins "before I realise I am doing it", is done "automatically", "without having to consciously remember" and "without thinking".

text.text: On each trial participants saw one of the eight vehicles used as discriminative stimuli in the task.
They had to indicate whether the correct response for that stimulus had been press or not press.

This answer was highlighted and then participants were required to answer one question on how difficult it would be to change that response ("This response is something … that would be difficult to change"), followed by the four questions from the SRBAI e.g.
"This response was something I did automatically".
Participants used a mouse to respond on a VAS scale ranging from 0 (completely disagree) to 100 (completely agree).
This process was repeated for each stimulus and the mean score was taken across the four SRBAI items, calculated separately for the NoGo and Go stimuli.
The experiment took place in a plain lab room.
Participants were told that they were going to play the "Sneaky Skateboard Game" where they were playing as a skateboarder and had to collect as many ice creams (and points) as possible.
The participant with the most points at the end of the study received cinema vouchers.
All participants started with 50 points.
Prior to the instrumental training phase participants completed a short demo with discriminative stimuli (vehicles) that did not appear in the real task.
During the demo participants learned that they should press the space bar in order to collect valuable pizza but should not respond when a vehicle associated with a not-valuable pizza was present.
After one block of the demo-training, they were also instructed about the test-phase.

Participants were told that the outcomes would no longer be visible because the drivers put an advertisement on top, and that the pizza's they had to collect differed from the first part of practice (i.e. some were devalued and some upvalued).
After conducting one block of demotest, they then began the instrumental training phase with ice creams.
In total, participants completed 36 training blocks, resulting in a total of 576 training trials and 72 stimulus-response repetitions per stimulus.
Every 6 blocks, participants were allowed to take a break of 30 seconds and could resume the task at any time during that period by pressing the space bar.

At the end of each block participants saw a screen with information on their performance, e.g. "75% correct PRESSES for ice creams that you DID have to collect. 65% correct NO PRESSES for ice creams that you DID NOT have to collect. 1 press that was too late.
You earned a total of 64 points!"
After the training phase, participants then answered the four questions from the SRBAI and the effort question for each discriminative stimulus that had appeared in the training phase.
At the beginning of the test phase, participants received instructions about the Numerical Stroop task (or control task) that they would be performing concurrently during the test phase.
They first completed two practice blocks with the Numerical Stroop task (or control task) and the same pizza scooters and outcomes as during the test-phase demo.
They were told that they should focus on performing well on the 'number game' and not worry about collecting the correct pizzas.
Next, participants were instructed that, just like before, they would be informed at the beginning of each block as to which ice creams they needed to collect.
However, they would have to rely on what they had already learned in the experiment because they would not be told on each trial which ice cream had been earned.
Instead, the vans delivering the ice creams had put an advertisement board on the roof and it was no longer possible to see the ice cream that each was carrying.
Participants were also told that they were still earning points for collecting valuable ice creams (and losing points for collecting not-valuable ice creams).
They were instructed that during the final phase all the vans would appear intermixed in each block.
They then completed four blocks of test trials (total of 128 trials total).
At the end of each block participants received feedback about their performance.
When participants had completed the four test blocks, they were informed as to the total points they had won.
Finally, they were asked to complete the demographics questionnaire.
Data analysis commenced after all data collection had been completed.

text.text: For valuable trials, response rates and accuracy are essentially the same metric, whereas on not-valuable trials Go responses are counted as errors.

This inconsistency between accuracy and response rates on not-valuable trials creates an unnecessary interaction between response rates and value in the response rate analysis, hence we chose to use accuracy instead.
By coding no-responses as accurate on NoGo trials the redundant four-way interaction in the test phase analysis is eliminated.

In addition, the expected metric of habitual responding should therefore be reflected as a main effect of congruency (less accurate on devalued relative to still-not-valuable and less accurate on upvalued relative to still-valuable outcomes).

The effect of memory-load on habitual responding should be reflected as a 2-way interaction between congruence and memory-load (with lower accuracy on devalued and upvalued trials for the memory-load group relative to the no-memory-load group).

Percentage accuracy during the training phase (i.e. number of responses made during the 600ms response window divided by number of trials * 100) was calculated separately for trials where stimuli signalled valuable versus not valuable outcomes.

This was analysed using repeated measures ANOVA with within-subject variables of block (1-6) and outcome value (valuable, not valuable) and the between-subject variable of memory-load group (memory-load vs. no-memory load).

The combination of the latter two variables gives the four trial types indicated previously: still valuable, still not valuable, upvalued and devalued.

Finally, we conducted a (preregistered) regression analysis.
As in our previous work, we calculated two difference scores for baseline-corrected performance on value-incongruent trials.
To calculate this 'habit score', we subtracted accuracy on devalued trials from stillnot-valuable trials and subtracted upvalued trial accuracy from that of still-valuable trials.
Greater difference scores represent more conflict on incongruent trials due to learned S-R associations.

These difference scores were then centred and used as the dependent variables in two regression models to determine whether the relationship between baseline working memory capacity and performance on the task was stronger under working memory load.

Normal probability plots and scatterplots of the standardized residuals were checked visually for violations of assumptions (including deviation from normality).

In Experiment 1, we used the SORT with a between-group working memory manipulation to assess whether imposing a memory load at test would impair goal-directed control and force reliance on S-R strategies compared to participants not under working memory load.
As expected, participants made more errors on value-incongruent trials, but the critical effect emerged on NoGo (devalued) trials.

Those under working-memory load were significantly impaired at withholding previously learned Go responses to stimuli signalling devalued outcomes (relative to those who were not under memory load), consistent with our preregistered predictions.

This finding indicates that taxing executive resources can reveal habitual responding in humans as reflected by increased slips of action towards for devalued outcomes, despite being counterproductive (leading to loss of points).
By contrast, working-memory load did not interfere with performance on not-valuable trials at test.
Regardless of working memory load condition, participants made more errors on value-incongruent (upvalued) trials relative to value-congruent (still-valuable) trials.

Importantly, errors on devalued and upvalued trials likely reflect different underlying mechanisms: failures to inhibit a prepotent (inhibiting a previously learned Go response) response on devalued trial versus failures to generate a novel response on upvalued trials.

As such, these error types need not be equally sensitive to working memory load (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Martínez-López et al., 2025; Rafei et al., 2026), a theme we return to in the general discussion.

text.text: This convergence across studies suggests that individual differences in cognitive resources contribute to the ability to adjust behaviour following changes in outcome value.

Importantly, participants accurately identified currently valuable outcomes at the start of each block, and explicit knowledge of stimulus-outcome contingencies was high and equivalent across memory-load groups.
This indicates that impaired performance on devalued trials was unlikely to reflect simple deficits in outcome value or contingency knowledge.

Instead, behaviour was no longer driven by the anticipation and evaluation of behavioural outcomes under working memory load, in line with the idea that well-learned S-R associations drove responding.

Experiment 2 aimed to replicate the findings of increased reliance on learned S-R associations when goal-directed control was taxed during the test phase.

This analysis suggested that a total sample size of n = 66 would be sufficient to replicate our analyses.

text.text: To complement the primary analysis, we conducted a Bayesian t-test analysis in JASP.
Bayes factor for the group difference in accuracy on still-not-valuable minus devalued trials (i.e. our habit index) was computed to examine support for the alternative versus null hypothesis.
The Bayes factor indicated moderate evidence for the directional alternative hypothesis, that reliance on habit would be stronger for those under concurrent memory load (BF+0 = 4.27).

In the present study we investigated whether a working memory load during an outcomerevaluation test could shift the balance between dual processes away from goal-directed control and allow habits to be more prominent.
To this end, we trained and tested participants on the SORT, with half receiving a concurrent working memory load task during the test phase.

Overall, participants made habitual slips-of-action on valueincongruent trials where the outcome value signalled by the stimulus had changed relative to training, requiring an adjustment of the learned response.
In line with our pre-registered hypotheses, we found across two experiments that those under working memory load performed significantly worse on the devalued test trials.
That is, participants in the memory-load group were impaired at inhibiting the learnt (Go) response to a stimulus that signalled a devalued outcome.
This central finding suggests that a working memory load can be used to reveal habits in humans; specifically, counterproductive responding for outcomes that are no longer valuable.
Working memory load also tended to affect performance on still-not-valuable trials, and the difference between groups was significant in the combined analysis.

However, both the final Bayesian analysis and the regression analysis from Experiment 1 demonstrated that even after controlling for NoGo performance on still-not-valuable trials, increased habit tendencies (specifically failures to inhibit prepotent Go responses) during the test phase were higher in those who were under working memory load.
Baseline working memory capacity also contributed independently to the regression model in Experiment 1 (after controlling for working memory load group assignment).
In line with our previous study, increased habit tendencies were associated negatively with baseline working memory capacity (Watson et al., 2023).

text.text: Overall, these findings were as expected: in situations where executive control functions were taxed, habits for devalued outcomes were more prominent.
Importantly, explicit knowledge of S/R-O associations at the end of the test was very high and there was no difference between memory-load groups.

The fact that poorer performance on value-incongruent trials was observed despite excellent explicit knowledge of the S-O relations, suggests that impaired behavioural flexibility on the value-incongruent trials cannot be attributed to diminished knowledge of the signalled outcome.
Instead, we argue that the memory load compromised the ability of participants to keep current goals and R-O contingencies active in working memory, and thereby increased reliance on S-R habits.

The fact that participants must learn the association between stimuli and outcomes in order to maximise reward during the training phase is an advantage of the SORT relative to the commonly used slips-of-action task (de Wit et al., 2012; Gillan et al., 2011).

text.text: Whereas Neal et al. demonstrated ecologically that cognitive depletion induced "in the wild" is associated with greater self-reported engagement in habitual behaviours, our results show that directly taxing working memory at the point of choice can shift action selection away from goal-directed control and toward habitual responding.
Following similar logic, imposing a memory load during training may promote an early reliance on S-R associations.

Consistent with this, stress manipulations applied during training have been shown to impair goal-directed control in outcome devaluation tasks (Schwabe & Wolf, 2009; but see: Smeets et al., 2023) and to bias behaviour toward model-free control in reinforcement learning paradigms (Gershman et al., 2014).

text.text: Future studies could add working memory load during training, to examine whether this promotes habit formation rather than only expression, while measuring contingency knowledge to determine whether this may be driven by stronger S-R learning or by impaired responseoutcome learning.
In addition, the dependence of habits on working memory availability could be further tested by varying the load of the working memory manipulation.

The results of the present study, where habits were more prominent when goal-directed resources were taxed by a working memory load, offer a promising new avenue for the investigation of the expression of habits.

text.text: We argued that goal-directed control dominated performance at test, obscuring the stronger habits that had built up for the long-trained stimuli during extended training (as reflected also in higher automaticity for long-trained Go stimuli).
The results of the present study, where working memory load promotes habitual control when goal-directed resources were taxed, support this notion.

That is -in the absence of working memory load or distraction -humans appear to be capable of readily shifting back to a goaldirected strategy when needed -perhaps not surprising when situated in an artificial laboratory environment and receiving explicit instructions about task-related changes that occur.
Future studies should combine the within-subjects overtraining manipulation with the memory-load manipulation.

Increased slips of action for overtrained stimuli may be observed when participants are under working memory load, thus providing direct evidence for stronger habits, as predicted by the associative dual-process model.

Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT) studies, Pavlovian stimuli that signal certain outcomes through stimulus-outcome (S-O) associations bias (separately trained) instrumental responses towards those same outcomes.
This PIT effect is thought to be mediated by S-O-R associations, or in other words: the Pavlovian stimuli activate responses via a shared outcome representation.

Interestingly, this PIT effect can take place even when the outcome is devalued (Corbit et al., 2007; Watson, Wiers, et al., 2018), suggesting that the instrumental response is selected based on anticipation of the outcome, but not on the evaluation of its current value.

text.text: Future research that can more directly distinguish between these mechanisms will be important for determining the basis of habitual behaviour following outcome revaluation under cognitive load.
In conclusion, we demonstrated that a working memory load shifted the balance of performance in an outcome-devaluation test from goal-directed control to habits.

While stimuli triggered slips of action towards no-longer-valuable outcomes in both memory load groups, participants who were under working memory load were relatively impaired at flexibly adjusting behaviour on the basis of changed outcome value, rendering them more dependent on learnt habits.
These findings suggest that during standard test conditions -in human research -goal-directed control dominates responding.

Imposing a working memory load renders test conditions more similar to real-life conditions, in which people often fall back on their habits when their working memory is taxed: e.g., because they are distracted, tired, stressed, or when they are multitasking.

The results of this study support the idea that researchers interested in studying (human) habits should tax goal-directed control to increase the ecological validity of the outcome-revaluation paradigm and thereby render it more sensitive to reveal the force of habits.

text.text: In total, 69 participants were recruited from the University of Amsterdam participant website, following the recruitment protocol of Experiment 1.
Six participants were excluded from all analyses (see results) leaving 63 participants in the analysis.
Demographic information for the remaining participants can be seen in Table 2.

text.text: The methods and procedure were as outlined in Experiment 1, except that participants did not complete the tests of baseline working memory capacity (i.e. digit span).

As pre-registered in Experiment 1, we excluded anyone who failed to achieve 80% accuracy in the last four block of instrumental training and/or those who had responded on less than 25% of the upvalued trials (stimuli whose associated outcome was valuable during test but had never been valuable during training).
This resulted in the exclusion of six participants.
Demographic data for the two memory load groups can be seen in Table 2.

text.text: Although we assessed participant's explicit knowledge of current outcome values (and thus the correct response) throughout the test phase, this was not done under time pressure or working memory load.
It is therefore not possible to rule out the possibility that during the test phase, incomplete or outdated S-O-R associations led to the observed performance under cognitive load.

Moreover, although the reduced accuracy on devalued trials under working-memory load is consistent with reduced outcome sensitivity, performance approached chance rather than showing a systematic bias towards the previously learned response.

Thus, the present findings do not necessarily indicate a complete shift from goal-directed to habitual control; rather, they likely reflect a reduced ability to use updated outcome information to discriminate between competing response

Although there is debate regarding the precise representational structure underlying goal-directed control (e.g., whether it is best characterised as S-O-R or S-R-O), we use the term O-R here as shorthand to denote behaviour that is mediated by an explicit representation of the outcome and its current value, in contrast to direct S-R control.
